transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Finova Head of ML), Aisha Khan (Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (SRE), Zoe Park (Data Privacy)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Today we wanted to walk through our prefix / prompt caching strategy, hit-rate modeling, and multi-tenant safety considerations. Priya and Maya will lead the technical bits.

[00:22] Priya (Redwood SE): Hi all, quick agenda: cache key design options, hit-rate math, eviction / TTL heuristics, security/isolation for VPC and on-prem, and practical benchmarks. We'll pause for questions.

[01:10] Carlos (Finova): Sounds good. Our main goals are reducing per-token cost for customer-facing pipelines and improving p95/p99 latency on chat. Also we have strict tenant isolation requirements.

[01:35] Maya (Redwood SE): Great. Starting with cache keys: we typically have three patterns we see in customers - full-prompt hash, prefix-only key, and structured key (metadata + prefix-hash). The tradeoffs: full-prompt gives perfect correctness but near-zero hit-rate; prefix-only gives good hit-rate but needs safety controls for leaking sensitive info.

[02:10] Aisha (Finova): When you say prefix, do you mean the first N tokens or a semantic prefix like the system prompt + user intent?

[02:20] Priya: Both options are used. We usually recommend system + fixed-length user prefix (e.g., first 64 tokens) as key, plus a canonicalization step (normalize whitespace, redact PII patterns). That balances hit-rate with safety.

[03:00] Liam (SRE): How do you handle collisions? I.e., different prompts mapping to same key because we truncated?

[03:12] Maya: We include a small probabilistic guard - metadata hashes and a short signature of the trailing context, and on a cache hit we validate by replaying the small suffix or checking a stored policy. If mismatch, we treat as miss. That reduces incorrect responses. There's a small CPU cost for validation but it's usually <2ms.

[04:05] Zoe (Data Privacy): I'm worried about multi-tenant data leakage. If you cache a prefix that includes tenant-specific identifiers, how do you ensure one tenant can't hit another's cached response?

[04:20] Priya: Good question. We enforce tenant scoping at the key namespace level: keys are namespaced by account id and deploy-mode. For hosted we zero-trust namespace per customer. For Dedicated/VPC we support per-tenant key prefixes and optional HMAC with customer-managed key so even if two tenants produce identical raw prefixes, keys differ. On on-prem, it's controlled by network access.

[05:00] Carlos: Is that HMAC with customer key the KMS integration you mentioned? How does it affect performance?

[05:10] Priya: Yes - optionally we sign keys with a KMS-backed HMAC. There's an extra network call if we do per-request signing, so we recommend local HMACs where possible (key cached in memory via HSM/KMS client) or batching key signing. Overhead is small compared to model inference, typically 1-4ms.

[06:00] Jordan: Let's talk hit-rates. What numbers do you expect?

[06:08] Maya: Hit-rate highly depends on workload. For assistant-style system prompts with repeated instructions, prefix caches often see 30-60% hit on tails. For chat with lots of customer-specific context, you might be 5-15%. We model expected token savings as hit_rate * avg_prefix_len / avg_total_len. In our internal benchmarks we saw 25-40% token reduction for common SaaS chat logs.

[07:05] Carlos: We have many templated prompts for our financial QA; maybe higher hit-rate. We can provide a sample set.

[07:22] Priya: That would help. Also important is how you choose TTL/eviction. Short TTLs favor freshness but lower hit-rate. For prompt caching we recommend tiered TTL: sticky keys for system/system-message prefixes (24h) and short TTL (5-30 minutes) for user-specific prefixes.

[08:05] Liam: Eviction policy—LRU? And what about memory pressure on multi-tenant hosts?

[08:15] Maya: We use approximate LRU with sharded in-memory stores + spillover to SSD. Per-tenant quota ensures noisy neighbors don't evict others. On Dedicated we allocate dedicated cache pool; in hosted mode we do multi-tenant pooling with soft and hard limits and tenant weights.

[09:00] Carlos: Can you shard keys by model version? We have rollouts and don't want stale model artifacts returned.

[09:10] Priya: Absolutely. Key namespace includes model_id and model_version. When you roll models we automatically namespace and warm the cache as part of canary rollout. If fallback occurs, we prefer newer model variant or follow configured policy.

[10:05] Jordan: Let's cover KV cache vs prefix cache - folks sometimes conflate the KV cache (decoder state) with prompt prefix caching (response reuse).

[10:20] Maya: Right. KV cache is the transformer’s key/value activations for the past tokens — that's per-request and used to speed autoregressive decoding. Prefix/prompt caching is storing complete model outputs for repeated prefixes to avoid kicking the model at all. They complement each other: prefix cache reduces number of inferences; KV caching speeds individual inferences and is important for streaming and low-latency long context.

[11:00] Aisha: For multi-tenant safety, are cached outputs considered customer data? What's retention policy?

[11:10] Priya: Yes, cached outputs are treated as customer data. We expose configs: retention TTL, encryption-at-rest, KMS key control in Private mode, and purge APIs. For hosted we offer per-account key and optional zero-retention config (no prefix cache persisted to disk).

[12:05] Zoe: We need SOC2 controls - audit logs saying who accessed or evicted keys. Do you surface that?

[12:15] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Console provides audit logs for cache ops as an optional retention add-on. We log cache hits/misses per key-id aggregated to avoid PII leakage, and admin actions are logged with user ids and timestamps.

[13:10] Carlos: On the hit-rate modeling, can you show the math?

[13:18] Maya: Sure. Example: avg_total_tokens=200, avg_prefix_tokens_cached=40, hit_rate=0.3 => token savings = 0.3 * 40 / 200 = 6%, but cost savings are higher because early return avoids entire decode for many tokens, and often prefixes contain high-probability/low-entropy tokens. Our benchmarks sometimes show 10-25% cost reduction for similar params. Priya has a spreadsheet with microbench numbers.

[14:10] Priya: I'll share that spreadsheet — it has permutations for prefix length, validation cost, and different miss probabilities.

[14:40] Liam: For eviction, do you allow manual pinning? E.g., pin welcome messages or regulatory content?

[14:48] Maya: Yes, we support pinning keys and TTL override via API. Also you can pre-warm caches during deploys.

[15:30] Carlos: What about quantization interactions? If a model is quantized differently across replicas, can a cached output from a quantized runtime be reused for a non-quantized runtime?

[15:42] Priya: Good catch. Cache namespacing must include runtime profile (quantization level, kernel selection). We include a runtime fingerprint in the key metadata to prevent cross-runtime reuse. We also support configurable relaxation where customers accept cross-runtime reuse if they accept small quality delta.

[16:30] Jordan: A question from sales: what are the expected latency improvements for tail p99?

[16:40] Maya: It depends. For workloads with high prefix reuse, we've observed p99 improvements of 200-600ms because we avoid full decode. For low reuse, benefit is negligible. Important to run customer-specific bench.

[17:10] Aisha: On VPC/on-prem, how do we validate isolation? We're planning a dedicated deployment in our VPC.

[17:22] Priya: For VPC and on-prem we recommend running the pilot with two tenants and a test harness that tries to hit cross-tenant keys. We'll also provide scripts to verify that key namespaces and HMAC keys differ. In Dedicated mode we can also allocate dedicated cache pools per tenant.

[18:05] Carlos: Any concerns about consistency — if we evict a key mid-flight do you return an error or recompute?

[18:14] Maya: We treat eviction as a miss for any new requests. If a cached response is served while eviction in progress, we ensure atomic semantics at the store level; there might be a tiny window but we avoid partial responses by storing complete payloads or object references.

[19:00] Jordan: Let's talk metrics to monitor.

[19:08] Priya: Key metrics: cache hit-rate by prefix-type, token-savings, CPU overhead for validation, per-tenant miss-rate, latency delta on hit vs miss, and abort/safety validation failures. We also recommend alerting when hit-rate drops suddenly (indicates prompt drift) or when validation failures spike.

[20:05] Carlos: Do you collect sample hits for debugging? We need to be careful about PII.

[20:15] Priya: By default we store only hashes and aggregated stats. For debugging you can opt-in to store redacted examples or ship them to your S3. We also provide regex-based scrubbing before any persistence.

[21:00] Maya: Quick note on implementation: we use a layered cache — L1 in-memory per-node, L2 distributed cache (rocksdb/SSD or clustered KV), with optional object storage for very large artifacts. L1 gives microsecond checks, L2 gives cross-node sharing.

[21:40] Liam: For multi-tenant noisy neighbor protection, you said per-tenant quotas. How strict? Can we reserve 30% of cache for our org?

[21:52] Priya: On Dedicated yes, you can reserve a pool. In hosted you can set weights and soft guarantees; absolute reservations are part of Dedicated or Private contracts.

[22:30] Carlos: Could we intentionally tokenize/prefix certain features to increase hit-rate, like normalizing user IDs out of prompts?

[22:42] Maya: Exactly — canonicalization is key. Replace identifiers with placeholders, normalize whitespace, and fold synonyms. That increases hit-rate without reducing correctness. We can help generate canonicalization rules from your sample prompts.

[23:50] Aisha: One operational question: how do you roll back if a cache policy causes quality regression?

[24:00] Jordan: We tie cache changes to canary rollouts. You can enable cache policy flags per route; we run A/B with and without cache and monitor your eval prompts for regressions. If we detect drift, automatic fallback to no-cache or conservative TTL happens.

[25:12] Carlos: Are there examples of false positive cache hits causing bad outputs?

[25:22] Maya: It can happen if keys are too coarse and we skip validation. In our early tests we had cases where personalization tokens were inadvertently included and caused cross-user output. That's why we recommend namespace + validation + conservative defaults.

[26:05] Priya: We'll also run synthetic tests: n-way collision tests and a red-team pass to try to provoke cross-tenant leakage. We provide the harness for that.

[27:00] Jordan: Let's quickly run through a proposed pilot: 2 weeks, 3 workloads (templated QA, user support chat, and internal analyst prompts). We'll instrument hit-rate, latency, and safety incidents. Priya will run bench variants: prefix-only, prefix+validation, and structured key.

[27:40] Carlos: Sounds good. We will supply sample prefixes and designate users for the tests.

[28:10] Maya: One more thing — when using quantized runtimes, we recommend keeping identical runtime fingerprint in cache to avoid repro differences.

[28:30] Zoe: Any legal / procurement notes? We will need a data processing addendum for retention and cache policies.

[28:40] Jordan: We'll attach standard DPA language and can add explicit cache retention clauses in the SOW.

[29:05] Priya: I'll summarize recommended defaults we use: canonicalize inputs, namespace by account+model+runtime, validation on hit with small suffix check, tiered TTLs (system 24h, user 5-30min), per-tenant quotas, optional HMAC signing for hosted keys.

[30:00] (30:00 - 62:00 minutes) - Q&A, deeper technical clarifications, and planning

[30:15] Aisha: For the suffix validation, what's the worst-case extra cost?

[30:24] Maya: Replaying small suffix of ~8-16 tokens to validate is about 3-8ms overhead in our environments if done locally; if it requires a remote check it could be higher.

[31:30] Carlos: If we do on-prem, can we run the cache entirely within our network?

[31:40] Priya: Yes — Private deployment allows local-only cache with your storage and encryption keys. We provide the same console telemetry optionally via a connector.

[32:20] Jordan: We'll share a design doc and the benchmark spreadsheet. Expect the doc to include concrete key schemas and examples.

[33:10] Carlos: For the spreadsheet, include permutations for prefix lengths 32/64/128, validation cost 2/5/10ms, and model sizes 7B/13B/70B.

[34:05] Priya: noted; that's exactly what we usually run.

[35:00] Maya: Recap of risk mitigation: namespace keys, HMAC/signing optional, validation on hit, scrub/redact before storage, per-tenant quotas, canary rollouts, and audit logs.

[36:00] Zoe: We'll need an attestation that keys are never used across tenants and proof during pilot.

[36:12] Jordan: We'll provide the attestation steps and verification scripts.

[37:00] Carlos: Anything else on batching interplay? How does prompt cache affect batching efficiency?

[37:10] Maya: Great point. Prompt caching reduces total inferences which can reduce batching opportunities, but overall cost usually drops. For steady-state high-throughput you may want both: respond with cache hits and for remaining live requests use batching. We also recommend hybrid batching where we keep small micro-batches to avoid increasing latency. Our autoscaler supports dynamic batch sizing depending on hit-rate.

[38:30] Aisha: Will we be able to toggle cache per-route?

[38:38] Priya: Yes, per-route config in the Redwood Console and via API.

[40:00] (Closing) Jordan: Thanks everyone. Next steps: Jordan sends design and security docs; Priya runs bench; Carlos provides prefixes; set pilot date. Any final questions?

[40:18] Carlos: No, thanks — looks good.

[40:25] Meeting ends.

Notes: Transcript contains transcription artifacts — some technical terms mistranscribed (e.g., kv cache as K-V cache, some punctuation missing). Links shared during call: https://redwood.example.com/prefix-caching-design (design doc), https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/prefix-cache-2025-02 (benchmark spreadsheet), shared via chat.
